prize_parts.citation: for the invention and development of the optical lattice clock, from the magic-wavelength trapping concept to clocks with fractional uncertainty at the 10^-18 level

statement.case_for: I have moved from B005 to B037. The decisive point is credit. The lattice clock splits into two identifiable contributions: Katori's magic-wavelength lattice, which cancels the light shift while many atoms are interrogated, and Ye's carrying of the strontium clock to the accuracy and stability frontier. No contributor of comparable standing is forced out by the three-person limit as Tu is in B005 or Zhang, Bernevig and Hughes are in B042. The result is independently reproduced and surpassed, and it is already used for gravitational-redshift tests, bounds on varying constants and dark-matter searches. Lindroth's argument shifted my view of novelty. Magic-wavelength trapping is a way of controlling internal and motional atomic states at once, and it opened collisional and many-body effects in clocks as a topic in its own right. That is more than a sharper instrument, and it fits an invention of importance in the sense of the Statutes. A narrow citation naming the magic-wavelength lattice and the 10^-18 regime keeps it distinct from the 2005 comb prize and the 2012 ion-control prize.
statement.case_against: My earlier objection has weakened but not gone. Precision measurement with atoms and lasers was recognised in 2005, 2012 and later, and a reader can fairly call this a fourth return to the neighbourhood. NIST, PTB, SYRTE and other lattice-clock groups are left outside a two-name prize, and I cannot judge from my own field how much of the 10^-18 record is Ye's group and how much is the wider community. The redefinition of the second is still pending. I treat that as confirmation of maturity, but it is a reasonable ground for waiting. Finally, I am leaving my own first choice, B005, for reasons that concern credit and support. It is not a judgment that the science is weaker. Statistical physics still has no prize for nonequilibrium collective phenomena, and that gap remains.

responses.point: Lindroth argues that magic-wavelength trapping is a conceptual step in controlling atomic internal and motional states, with many-body physics in lattice clocks following from it, and not only metrology.
responses.response: This is the argument that moved me. In round 1 I asked what new principle the clock adds beyond the magic-wavelength idea. Your answer is that the idea is the principle: it allows many atoms in a Lamb-Dicke lattice with the clock transition left unperturbed, and the collisional shifts, spin squeezing and interaction effects then become physics in their own right. I accept that as an invention of importance. I also thank you for your comment on active matter. The Tu omission is the point on which I now concede, so I have not kept B005 as my first choice.

responses.point: Danielsson asks whether the Vicsek model and the continuum Toner-Tu theory are one achievement or two, since that decides whether a three-name list can be defended honestly for B005.
responses.response: They are two achievements. Vicsek's simulations show the flocking transition numerically, while Toner and Tu's hydrodynamics explains why long-range order can exist in two dimensions, and Ramaswamy's work on suspensions is a third line. Three names map onto three contributions only if Tu is dropped from the second, and I do not think that is defensible, since the theory carries his name. You are right that this is structural. Together with the lack of support from any other member, it is why I am withdrawing B005 as my preferred part. I keep it as an alternative because I think the committee will need to return to the field.

responses.point: Pearce says the central Toner-Tu prediction of long-range order in two dimensions has not been tested well enough, that Tu's omission is substantive, and that B005 has no route to a majority. He also keeps B042 as his preferred part.
responses.response: I accept all three points and have acted on them. On B042, I still regard it as the strongest fallback on maturity, but the HgTe proposal came from Bernevig, Hughes and the late Zhang, and your own statement concedes that quantisation in the helical edge is less clean than in the quantum Hall effect. Citations cannot repair that for Zhang. I would be more comfortable with B042 if the wording stated openly what it does not claim, as the chair asked. I still prefer B037, whose credit divides more cleanly, and I do not think B042's weaknesses exceed B037's. I do not claim B042 is the weaker science.

responses.point: Kroll supports B037 with Katori credited for the concept and first demonstrations and Ye for the accuracy record, and he acknowledges the proximity to the 2005 and 2012 prizes.
responses.response: I accept your credit split and the guard against your own taste as a spectroscopist. The question I would put to you is whether Ye is credited for the lattice clock or for clock-comb integration and the accuracy frontier. I read the citation as the second, with Katori named for the concept, and I support wording that says so and does not imply that Ye invented the magic-wavelength lattice. I would also favour a sentence in the text acknowledging the NIST, PTB and SYRTE groups, since you are right that they are outside the two names.

uncertainties: Whether the committee will read the lattice clock as an invention distinct from the 2005 comb and 2012 ion-control prizes, or as an incremental advance in an area recognised several times.
How much of the 10^-18 record belongs to Ye's group and how much to other laboratories, and whether the citation can express this without overclaiming.
Whether the pending redefinition of the second should be a reason to wait or confirmation of maturity.
Whether my move from B005 is a defensible judgment on credit and support or an overcorrection, since the science of active matter is still of the first rank.
statement.conflict_note: No specific personal or institutional conflict is apparent from the provided profile. Active matter and stochastic dynamics lie close to my own research interests, but none of Toner, Ramaswamy or Vicsek appears among my documented co-authors or institutional connections, and I no longer prefer B005. I have no documented connection to Katori, Ye or their groups, or to the Kane, Mele and Molenkamp candidates. I rely only on the supplied evidence and do not claim any undocumented relationship.
